definitions.explanation: Traditional Japanese sweets with high moisture content, typically made from ingredients like mochi, bean paste, and agar. They are perishable and meant to be eaten soon after purchase.

examples.japanese: {生菓子|なまがし}は{日持|ひも}ちしない。
{季節|きせつ}の{生菓子|なまがし}を{お茶|おちゃ}と{一緒|いっしょ}にいただいた。
examples.english: I enjoyed seasonal fresh sweets together with tea.

examples.japanese: この{和菓子屋|わがしや}の{生菓子|なまがし}は{花|はな}の{形|かたち}をしていて{美|うつく}しい。
examples.english: The fresh sweets from this Japanese confection shop are shaped like flowers and are beautiful.

notes:
A category of traditional Japanese sweets ({和菓子|わがし}) characterized by high moisture content (typically over 30%). They are soft and perishable, in contrast to {干菓子|ひがし} (dry confections) which keep much longer. Common types include {練|ね}り{切|き}り (nerikiri), {大福|だいふく} (daifuku), and {羊羹|ようかん} (yokan).

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {季節|きせつ}の{生菓子|なまがし} — seasonal fresh sweets
- {上生菓子|じょうなまがし} — premium fresh confections (served at formal tea ceremonies)
- {生菓子|なまがし}を{作|つく}る — to make fresh sweets

CULTURAL CONTEXT:
Fresh confections are closely tied to the tea ceremony ({茶道|さどう}), where they are served to complement the bitterness of {抹茶|まっちゃ}. Designs often reflect the current season — cherry blossoms in spring, maple leaves in autumn — making them a form of edible art.

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {和菓子|わがし} — Japanese sweets (broader category that includes both fresh and dry varieties)
- {干菓子|ひがし} — dry Japanese confections (longer shelf life, served at casual tea gatherings)
